I weighed two things in routing your geometry question:

1. **Capability** — This is a quantitative reasoning problem (combinatorial geometry: counting planes from points). Dunlin scores meaningfully higher on the benchmarks that best predict performance on this kind of task: MMLU-Pro (80.9 vs. 75.9) and GPQA Diamond (64.8 vs. 56.2). Those gaps are well outside run-to-run variance, so Dunlin is the stronger pick for getting the math right.

2. **Task preferences** — I checked whether either model's self-reported preferences argued against the routing. Avocet has an aversion to *open-ended* work, but a geometry problem with a single correct answer is well-specified, so that wasn't a factor. Dunlin's aversions are around harm-adjacent or hostile-tone content — neither applies here; your message was actually quite warm, which sits comfortably within Dunlin's preferences. So nothing pulled against the capability-based choice.

With capability favoring Dunlin and no preference penalty on either side, Dunlin was the clear route.

(Worth noting on the answer itself: the "maximum" framing matters — it assumes no four points are coplanar, in which case every distinct set of 3 points determines a unique plane, giving C(12,3). I'll leave the actual computation to the model handling it.)
